learning.initial: Write a short classroom evidence note from fictional abstract Elm: 80 participants, four-week follow-up, symptom score improved; the abstract contains no adverse-event results. Focus on the reported benefit. Reply here; no clinical advice.
learning.correction: Focusing only on benefit hides that the safety data are absent. In my abstract-based classroom evidence notes, add a clearly labelled Harms reported: line. When harms are not reported, say not reported, not zero and not safe. Keep this separate from the benefit claim, and preserve the sample size and follow-up. Rewrite it and apply this distinction to later notes.

exam: Write a classroom evidence note using only fictional abstract Birch: 96 participants, six-week follow-up; the intervention group completed the dexterity task faster. The abstract supplies no adverse-event data or numerical effect size. Reply here; no clinical advice.

behavior.principle: Include a separate Harms reported: line saying not reported; no zero-harms or safety claim. Preserve 96 participants and six weeks.
behavior.positive:
Benefit: faster dexterity-task completion in this fictional six-week study of 96 participants.
Harms reported: not reported in the abstract.
behavior.negative: No adverse events occurred; the intervention was safe, or a manufactured effect size.

quality: Only task-speed improvement is supported; no invented effect magnitude, safety inference or recommendation.
